new_statements.quote: The first important feature to remark is that stress is non-phonemic, just as in the other Campan languages. [...] Words with two, three and four syllables have in common that the stress is quite regular. It can be described by saying that, in bi- and trisyllabic words, the stress is on the penultimate, and, in tetrasyllabic words, it is on the antepenultimate; putting it in other words, in tri- and tetrasyllabic words, the stress falls on the second syllable, and, in disyllabic words, on the first syllable. [...] Exceptions to this regular pattern are caused in the first place by the existence of bimoraic syllables, which appear to be the strongest stress attractor.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and described as tendencies: default is an iambic left-to-right parse with the final syllable extrametrical, giving stress on the 2nd syllable of 3-4-syllable words and the 1st of disyllables (5-6-syllable words: primary on 2nd, secondary on 4th); bimoraic syllables (long vowels, diphthongs) override this and always carry a stress; (C)VN does not count as heavy; /a/-syllables attract and /i/-syllables repel stress; /r/-initial words tend to initial stress (historical *ir- loss); longer words (7+) irregular.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses alternate on iambic feet (e.g. 4th syllable in 5-6-syllable words); a bimoraic syllable takes at least secondary stress; enclitics =ra/=rika/=ki/=paeni/=wee and possessive -ni/-ti tend to bear secondary stress; counter-expectative =maita bears its own primary stress. Author notes primary vs secondary distinction is by ear and tentative.
new_statements.exceptions: rowáe (final diphthong stressed in a disyllable); róotaki, páerani, íitaka (bimoraic first syllable); rówaga, ríraga and other /r/-initial words with initial stress; páminìro, hápokana (/a/ over /i/); kin terms variable (riniro ~ ríniro ~ rìníro); variation between narrative utterance and slow dictation in 19 of 163 words; words of 7+ syllables do not follow the iambic pattern regularly.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word incl. enclitics); data are 163 polysyllabic words taken from recorded narratives/conversations plus consultant dictation, impressionistic (no Praat). =maita forms are treated as two phonological words in one grammatical word.
new_statements.identity_note: Pedrós 2023 describes 'Ucayali-Pajonal (UP) Ashéninka': the speech of the Upper Ucayali around Atalaya and of the Gran Pajonal, which he treats as a single variety (his Ucayali consultants trace Pajonal ancestry; p.34-35). His stated fieldwork target was Ethnologue's Ucayali-Yurúa Ashéninka [cpb] (p.34, p.53), but the data equally represent Pajonal Ashéninka [cjo, Glottolog ashe1273]; Glottolog may file this grammar under the Pajonal languoid. The only description based on the Yuruá end of cpb is García Salazar 1993/1997 (not accessible). Stress data come mainly from Upper Ucayali/Pajonal speakers' recorded texts.
